newsitem.title: FRANCE: Focus-France ready to lose majority in Thomson-CSF.
newsitem.headline: Focus-France ready to lose majority in Thomson-CSF.

text.p: France's new left-wing government signalled on Wednesday it was ready to surrender its majority in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, opening the way to outside alliances while the state keeps an important stake.
Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said no decisions had been taken on the future of Europe's top defence electronics supplier, whose planned privatisation was abandoned on Friday.

But he gave the first cabinet indication that the Socialist-led government was considering letting its 58 percent stake fall below half way to allow private partners a role in fending off international defence competition.

"(When you start) with 58 percent, if you want to create an alliance with a partner it is difficult to keep around 50 percent," Strauss-Kahn told reporters after a closed-door hearing of the parliament's defence committee.
"That is why the prime minister has talked of a decisive stake and not a majority stake," he said.

Prime Minister Lionel Jospin on Friday cancelled plans by his centre-right predecessors to sell the state's 58 percent stake. His office said a new project to muster a French defence electronics group around a "decisive" public share in Thomson-CSF would be launched soon, but gave no details.

French newspapers have speculated this would involve the government dropping its participation in Thomson-CSF to 40 percent, perhaps as little as 33 percent, by bringing in new capital but without selling off any public stock directly.
Most reports say the leading candidate for a minority place in the new structure is engineering firm Alcatel, but its bitter rival Lagardere calls this premature.
Both had competed for full control in the abandoned selloff.
Strauss-Kahn did not rule out lowering the state's share to 33 percent, the minimum needed for a blocking minority, but stressed this was not the only proposal worth considering.
"It's a good solution but there are other possibilities. Nothing has been decided," he said. He hoped a decision on opening up the company's capital would be taken by end-year.
That will please Britain's GEC-Marconi, whose chairman Geoffrey Pattie said in Paris on Wednesday he was ready to do deals with public firms but hoped for a rapid outcome.
Missiles maker Lagardere, meanwhile, said it would not go ahead with a planned issue of 5.5 billion francs in special bonds needed to finance its original privatisation bid.
The bonds would have been paid back in Thomson-CSF shares.
Shares in Thomson-CSF recovered two percent to 167 francs after falling sharply on Tuesday. Alcatel was a touch lower at 771 francs while Lagardere rose almost one percent to 176.1.
A final decision on the future of Thomson-CSF now depends on Jospin, whose office has taken direct control over the sensitive privatisation dossier.

Conservative President Jacques Chirac criticised the government's policies on privatisation and other issues on Monday, prompting a stern call from Jospin on Wednesday for respect for the constitution.
Under "cohabitation", or power-sharing between a president and prime minister of different politicial parties, the president controls foreign policy, leaving domestic policy to the government.
